eligibility_reason: HierarCache, one of AgentSafe's two named components, is an 'adaptive memory management system' (p. 1) that agents write to at run time: the memory update function U(vi,vj,m,ℓ) adds each communicated message m to a security-level memory set Mℓ, or to a junk set, as agents interact over 5-50 rounds (p. 5). A periodic detection mechanism R(vj,t) re-assesses stored entries and removes invalid ones from Mℓ into junk memory (p. 6), so the store is both written and later acted upon within the same multi-turn agent interaction the experiments measure (p. 5, Table 1). Year 2025, English, full text present — I2/I3/I4 all hold. No exclusion applies: this is not hardware/cache-only (not E1), the store is externalized and agent-written, not parametric-only (not E2), the agent writes the store rather than querying a fixed corpus (not E3), it is primary research with experiments, not a survey (not E4), memory management is one of the two claimed contributions, not incidental (not E5), it is an LLM-based multi-agent system (not E6), and the paper runs well past four pages with full experiments (not E7).

facets.justification: The paper's own description does not map onto the listed categories: 'HierarCache can further be understood as a hierarchical database that allocates relationship-based access permissions' (p. 2), organizing memory 'into multiple layers, each corresponding to a specific security level, and includes an additional "junk" memory layer' (p. 5). No schema/SQL-style query is described (not relational_db), no embeddings-based similarity search over the stored items themselves is described (the vector similarity on p. 5 is used only inside the write-time detection function D(m), not for retrieval), and it is not nodes/edges, files, prompt-resident text, or KV-cache state.

Beyond adding messages to Mℓ (Eq. 7, p. 5), the periodic detection mechanism actively corrects the store: 'if Fℓ is a subset of Mℓ, then Mℓ is updated by removing Fℓ from it (Mℓ ← Mℓ\Fℓ)... all sets Fℓ ... are added to Mjunk' (p. 6, Eq. 12). This deletion/relocation of existing entries based on newly generated validity judgments is what Appendix H specifically validates ('Validation for Periodic Detection Mechanism', Table 5, p. 20), making correction of existing entries the evaluated transformation rather than plain append.

Missing: the extracted pages (1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 19, 20, 21) describe how HierarCache decides what to write, verify, and evict (Eqs. 7-12, pp. 5-6) but do not describe a mechanism by which a stored message re-enters an agent's context for a later decision — no query, similarity-retrieval, recency window, or agent-issued read action over Mℓ is specified on any given page. The security-level partitioning governs write placement and access permission, not a stated read/retrieval procedure, so this axis cannot be decided from what was given.

The authors state their own aim as validation: 'we conduct extensive experiments to validate the effectiveness of AgentSafe in various attack scenarios and datasets' (p. 2). Evidence is produced on two constructed datasets, RIOH and WCEI (p. 6), across several LLM APIs, comparing 'AgentSafe' against a 'w/o AgentSafe' baseline (Table 1, p. 5) — a controlled lab comparison, not a fielded system with real users or real stakes. The abstract's closing claim of 'potential for real-world application' (p. 1) signals aspiration rather than a deployment already studied, so this is coded conservatively as validation rather than evaluation.

Defense success rates are reported across two datasets (RIOH, WCEI), four attack methods, and ten interaction-turn checkpoints against a fixed baseline, for multiple LLMs (Llama 3.2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4) (Table 1, p. 5; p. 6). This is a fixed task suite with quantitative scores reported per condition, matching benchmark_evaluation; the Appendix G/H ablation and periodic-detection comparisons (pp. 19-20) follow the same dataset/score-table structure rather than a single isolated manipulated-variable experiment.

The abstract introduces AgentSafe as 'a novel framework that enhances MAS security through hierarchical information management and memory protection' (p. 1), and the contribution list frames it architecturally: 'First Security-Level-Based MAS... enabling hierarchical information management' and 'HierarCache Design. We introduce the philosophy of a HierarCache' (p. 2). Code is released on GitHub (p. 1), but the paper argues for the layered security architecture itself, not the released artefact as the contribution.
